summary:
Nigeria criminalises same-sex conduct nationally under the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 (SSMPA), and the law reaches far beyond marriage. Human Rights Watch (October 2016), in the report 'Tell Me Where I Can Be Safe', documents that it bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, carrying 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and records police torture and arbitrary arrests carried out under it.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) assesses that same-sex sex between men is criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and that Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalises same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions.

Official foreign guidance aimed at LGBT+ visitors is explicit and current. Sahara Reporters (August 2026), reporting the latest UK FCDO travel advice for Nigeria, relays warnings of attacks, blackmail and intimidation against LGBT+ travellers, up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states.

Trans visitors face lethal violence with official misgendering and subsequent impunity. The beaten body of the Abuja trans TikToker 'Abuja Area Mama', a 33-year-old transgender woman, was found on a highway in Abuja in August 2024, hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; police said preliminary investigations showed 'a man fully dressed in female clothing', and the Abuja police chief ordered a 'thorough and discreet' investigation. Six months later, in February 2025, The Dial reported that no suspects had been charged.

Police use the law against people for how they appear. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that a 24-year-old man, Okafor, was stopped by Lagos police, struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and freed only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for 'looking gay'; those affected describe the SSMPA as a weaponised law creating a climate of hostility.

Dating applications carry a specific entrapment risk. Context/Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents 'kito' gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and other apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

A decade-outcome assessment of the statute exists. Context/Thomson Reuters Foundation (August 2024), marking ten years of the SSMPA, finds the 2014 law has fuelled violence, extortion and discrimination far beyond its scope and has effectively sanctioned abuse, with LGBTQ+ Nigerians reporting lost job prospects and increased attacks since it passed.

Enforcement takes the form of mass arrests at social venues. Wikipedia's country coverage records that men arrested in Bauchi in August 2007 were held for several years awaiting a trial that dissolved by end-2011; that 100-plus party-goers were arrested at a hotel in Asaba, Delta State, in June 2018; 57 young men at Egbeda, Lagos, in August 2018; the 'Warri 67' in Warri, Delta State, in August 2023; and 76 people arrested at a party in Gombe state in October 2023. LGBTQ-friendly venues face closure: the House of Rainbow Metropolitan Church in Lagos cancelled conferences after members' names and addresses were published in four newspapers on 12 September 2008 and some were threatened, beaten and stoned.

Cross-dressing has been proposed as a discrete offence. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians fear proposals to criminalise cross-dressing.

Imprisonment of a prominent transgender woman raised placement questions that remain unresolved. Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye) pleaded guilty to four counts of Naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine; she served the term in Kirikiri maximum-security prison, Lagos, and was released on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison would hold 'the crossdresser', reflecting discretionary placement. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that placing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

Care access is chilled by arrest and extortion risk. Many LGBTQ Nigerians fear seeking medical care or reporting crimes, and activists say the Same-Sex Marriage Prohibition Act hampers access to HIV prevention services and forces LGBTQ people and allies to abandon community health and education work.
tangentialFactors:
The Constitution, section 17(3)(d), nominally guarantees adequate medical and health care to all citizens, yet a 2015 survey by Bisi Alimi's organisation found that only 30% of Nigerians agree LGBTQ persons should receive education, healthcare and housing. The gap between the written guarantee and measured public opinion shapes how safely a visitor can expect to be treated in institutional settings.

The Federal Ministry of Education maintains a national policy on safety, security and violence-free schools in all Nigerian schools that prohibits discrimination explicitly including on 'sexual orientation'. No enacted legislation protects against discrimination generally, and no political party endorses LGBTQ rights, so the school policy sits without a statutory counterpart elsewhere in public life.

Religious institutions are a principal driver of the environment. Mainstream interpretations of Islam and Christianity are said to drive stigmatisation of LGBTQ students, and religious institutions play a crucial role in education, which is relevant to how public-facing hostility is framed.

The 2008 publication of House of Rainbow members' names and addresses in four newspapers shows that press exposure of individuals has previously produced threats, beatings and stonings, an earlier pattern that predates the 2014 statute.
localsOnly:
LGBTQ Nigerians report lost job prospects since the SSMPA passed, and attacks increased over the decade to 2024, with the law described by those affected as effectively sanctioning abuse.

Community counter-measures to 'kito' entrapment include exposure forums and sting operations, with one administrator's alert page drawing 43,000 followers.

Residents arrested in the Bauchi sweep of August 2007 were held in jail for several years awaiting a trial that dissolved by end-2011, an illustration of pre-trial detention duration in these cases.

Activists state that the SSMPA hampers access to HIV prevention services and compels LGBTQ people and their allies to leave community health and education work. NGOs Global Rights and The Independent Project provided LGBT groups with HIV/AIDS awareness training, recorded in a 2011 US State Department report.

Many LGBTQ Nigerians avoid seeking medical care or reporting crimes to police because of arrest risk and 'kito' extortion.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Bobrisky was assigned to a male or a female section of Kirikiri prison is not recorded in the available source; press coverage raised the question of placement without resolving it, and the October 2024 panel addressed only the lawfulness of the prison classification, not the section.

The inventory does not indicate whether the 2022 proposals to criminalise cross-dressing reported by Reuters have been enacted, so their current legal status is unresolved here.

No enacted general legislation protecting against discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation or gender identity is sourced; the education ministry's school policy is administrative rather than statutory, and its practical enforcement is not documented in these materials.

Entry, visa and gender-marker document rules for visitors are not covered by any source in this inventory and remain not sourced.

Several of the arrest totals and biographical details are drawn from tertiary reference coverage rather than primary court records, and the charge and sentence dates for Bobrisky are reported without a linked judgment.
